Quick Summary

Slouching Towards Bethlehem is a collection of essays by Joan Didion, published in 1968. It is known for its lucid prose and its examination of social unrest and psychological fragmentation, particularly in relation to the 1960s counterculture in California. The title essay, which takes its name from a poem by W.B. Yeats, offers a critical look at the Haight-Ashbury hippie scene in San Francisco. Didion's work is a prominent example of New Journalism , a style that blended literary techniques with factual

Joan Didion

Slouching Towards Bethlehem

1968

For Quintana

Turning and turning in the widening gyre

The falcon cannot hear the falconer;

Things fall apart; the center cannot hold;

Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world,

The blood-dimmed tide is loosed, and everywhere

The ceremony of innocence is drowned;

The best lack all conviction, while the worst

...

Troubles my sight: somewhere in the sands of the desert

A shape with lion body and the head of a man,

A gaze blank and pitiless as the sun,

Is moving its slow thighs, while all about it

...

be born?

W. B. YEATS

I learned courage from Buddha, Jesus, Lincoln, Einstein, and Cary Grant.

—MISS PEGGY LEE

A Preface

THIS BOOK is called Slouching Towards Bethlehem because for several years

now certain lines from the Yeats poem which appears two pages back have reverberated in my inner ear as if they were surgically implanted there. The widening gyre, the falcon which does not hear the falconer, the gaze blank and pitiless as the sun; those have been my points of reference, the only images against which much of what I was seeing and hearing and thinking seemed to make any pattern. “Slouching Towards Bethlehem” is also the title of one piece in the book, and that piece, which derived from some time spent in the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco, was for me both the most imperative of all these pieces to write and the only one that made me despondent after it was printed.
